note:
ISO 2026-W51 runs from December 14 through December 20. Mercury is about 1.9° in ecliptic longitude from Antares in Scorpius. To find Jupiter, first identify Leo, trace the Sickle, and locate Regulus in that pattern. Jupiter lies about 2.8° away in ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot; use the finder to transfer from Regulus to the planet.

**Naked eye:** 🌓 First Quarter — 05:42:40 UTC. Moderate moonlight makes timing and local sky position important for faint targets. Use Polaris as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -8.4; direct motion; 20.5% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Saturn in ecliptic longitude Dec 18 05:20 UTC. Conjunction with Neptune in ecliptic longitude Dec 17 17:35 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude -0.7; direct motion; 96.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -4.8; direct motion; 37.7% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 0.2; direct motion; 90.7% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Ceres: Binoculars; magnitude 7.3; retrograde motion; 99.1% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Jupiter: Naked eye; magnitude -2.3; retrograde motion; 99.3% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.7; direct motion; 99.7% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Dec 18 05:20 UTC. Uranus: Binoculars; magnitude 5.6; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.7; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Dec 17 17:35 UTC. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.6; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot.

**Binoculars:** Trace the charted figure of For, then identify β For at its plotted position.

**Small telescope:** MCG 0-7-17: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Arp 135: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M34: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M77: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; NGC 1097: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

**Substantial telescope:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified as requiring a substantial telescope this week.

story_candidates.dek: MCG 0-7-17 is an observing target in Cet carried by the weekly Calendar.
story_candidates.body:
Why it is here: The Calendar selected MCG 0-7-17 as one of this week’s fixed-sky observing targets.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Cet constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

story_candidates.dek: Polaris is a star in UMi of catalogue visual magnitude 1.97; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
The stored catalogue gives a visual magnitude of 1.97. This is a catalogue value, not a prediction of its brightness this week. Lower magnitudes mean brighter objects; sky brightness and altitude affect whether you can see the star.

Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 2h 31m and declination +89.3°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star is circumpolar (at 45° declination it touches the geometric horizon at lower culmination). It reaches approximately 46° altitude at upper culmination. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved UMi constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.
